title: Intelligent Tutoring Goes To School in the Big City
authors: Kenneth R. Koedinger, John R. Anderson, William H. Hadley, Mary A. Mark
abstract: This paper reports on a large-scale experiment introducing and evaluating intelligent tutoring in an urban High School setting. Critical to the success of this project has been a client-centered design approach that has matched our client's expertise in curricular objectives and classroom teaching with our expertise in artificial intelligence and cognitive psychology. The Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project (PUMP) has produced an algebra curriculum that is centrally focused on mathematical analysis of real world situations and the use of computational tools. We have built an intelligent tutor, called PAT, that supports this curriculum and has been made a regular part of 9th grade Algebra in 3 Pittsburgh schools. In the 1993-94 school year, we evaluated the effect of the PUMP curriculum and PAT tutor use. On average the 470 students in experimental classes outperformed students in comparison classes by 15% on standardized tests and 100% on tests targeting the PUMP objectives. This study provides further evidence that laboratory tutoring systems can be scaled up and made to work, both technically and pedagogically, in real and unforgiving settings like urban high schools.
explain_beginner: This paper describes a project that brought a computer tutor into real high school algebra classes in a big city. Teachers helped design the tutor and the curriculum, so it fit their goals and teaching style. In one school year, about 470 students used the tutor. These students scored 15 percent better than other classes on standard tests, and twice as well on tests about the specific topics they studied. The finding matters because it shows that computer tutoring can work in ordinary, busy city schools, not just in small experiments.
explain_business: This study shows that a computer-based algebra tutor, developed with teachers rather than imposed on them, improved student performance in real urban high schools. Students using it scored 15 percent higher on standardized tests and twice as high on curriculum-specific tests. For decision makers, the lesson is that intelligent tutoring can be deployed at scale in ordinary classrooms and still produce measurable gains. It supports investing in tools co-designed with educators, and it suggests such systems can be a practical way to raise math achievement in large school districts.
explain_practitioner: The authors report a large-scale evaluation of an intelligent algebra tutor, PAT, embedded in the Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project curriculum, which emphasizes real world analysis and computational tools. The tutor was created through a client-centered design process, combining teacher curricular and classroom expertise with AI and cognitive psychology knowledge. PAT became part of regular 9th grade algebra in three Pittsburgh schools. In 1993-94, 470 experimental students outperformed comparison classes by 15 percent on standardized tests and 100 percent on PUMP-targeted tests, demonstrating technical and pedagogical scalability in urban high schools.
